stem: A public-facing API's Lambda function must respond with consistent low double-digit-millisecond latency on every invocation, including the very first one after a new deploy. Which TWO approaches address that cold start specifically? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Increasing the function's timeout setting to the maximum
AWS Compute Optimizer's Lambda memory recommendation
Increasing the function's memory setting alone

rationale: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a chosen number of execution environments so invocations skip the cold-start Init phase entirely, giving consistent response times including the first request. Lambda SnapStart resumes new environments from an already-initialized snapshot instead of re-running startup code, cutting cold starts to as low as sub-second for supported runtimes. Increasing the function's timeout only changes how long a single invocation may run before Lambda terminates it; it does not pre-initialize any execution environment and has no effect on Init-phase cold-start latency. Compute Optimizer's memory recommendation is about right-sizing cost and duration from utilization history, not about eliminating a cold start. Increasing memory alone can shorten execution once a function is running, but it does not remove the Init-phase cold start on a fresh environment the way provisioned concurrency or SnapStart does.
